procedural_history.originating_court: IInd Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gautam Budh Nagar, U.P.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 23.10.2019 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Misc. Application No. 471 of 2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Misc. Application No. 471 of 2018 before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, seeking to quash the proceedings against him. The High Court passed an order on 23.10.2019, the contents of which are not specified in the provided text, but it was unfavorable to the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order dated 23.10.2019. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing the High Court's order and also quashing the FIR dated 4.9.2016, the chargesheet filed, and the summoning order dated 19.09.2017 passed by the IInd Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gautam Budh Nagar, U.P., but only with respect to the appellant.

directions: The order dated 23.10.2019 passed by the High Court in Criminal Misc. Application No. 471 of 2018 qua the appellant is quashed and set aside.

FIR dated 4.9.2016 bearing Case Crime No. 839 of 2016 as also the chargesheet ﬁled in Case Crime No. 839 of 2016 under Sections 323, 384 and 406 of the I.P.C. and the summoning order dated 19.09.2017 in case No.2986 of 2017 passed by the learned IInd Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Gautam Budh Nagar, U.P., stand quashed, qua the appellant herein.

issue.issue_text: Whether the chargesheet submitted showed prima facie case u/ss. 323, 384 and 406, IPC for voluntarily causing hurt, for extortion and for criminal breach of trust;

facts: A chargesheet was filed against the appellant for offenses under Sections 323 (voluntarily causing hurt), 384 (extortion), and 406 (criminal breach of trust) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The Supreme Court carefully reviewed the chargesheet and all other materials on record to determine if a prima facie case existed for these offenses.
law: To establish an offense under Section 323 IPC (voluntarily causing hurt), there must be material evidence to support the allegation of hurt being caused.

To establish an offense under Section 384 IPC (extortion), two key ingredients must be present: (i) intentionally putting a person in fear of injury, and (ii) dishonestly inducing that person to deliver property or a valuable security.

To establish an offense under Section 406 IPC (criminal breach of trust), the essential ingredients are: (i) entrustment of property to a person, and (ii) dishonest misappropriation or conversion of that property by the person entrusted.
application: For the Section 323 charge, the court found only a "bald statement" from the complainant that "they beat up me." There was no other supporting material, such as an injury report, evidence of medical treatment, or even a statement that the complainant saw a doctor.

For the Section 384 charge, the court found that the chargesheet did not contain the necessary accusations to satisfy the twin ingredients of putting someone in fear of injury and dishonestly inducing them to deliver property.
For the Section 406 charge, the court determined that the basic ingredient of "entrustment of property" was absent from the case materials, making it impossible to attract the offense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the chargesheet and the materials on record failed to establish the necessary legal ingredients for the offenses under Sections 323, 384, and 406 of the IPC. Consequently, it found that no prima facie case was made out against the appellant and rejected the charges.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court has fallen in error in not invoking the powers u/s. 482, Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings qua the appellant.

facts: An FIR was registered against the appellant and his family, and a chargesheet was later filed for offenses under Sections 323 (voluntarily causing hurt), 384 (extortion), and 406 (criminal breach of trust) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The appellant filed an application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) before the High Court, seeking to quash the criminal proceedings.
The High Court dismissed the application and declined to quash the proceedings against the appellant.
The appellant then appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court.
law: Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. grants the High Court inherent power to quash criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of court or to secure the ends of justice.
Section 323, IPC requires evidence of voluntarily causing hurt.
Section 384, IPC requires two ingredients: (i) intentionally putting a person in fear of injury, and (ii) dishonestly inducing that person to deliver property.
Section 406, IPC requires: (i) entrustment of property to a person, and (ii) dishonest misappropriation or conversion of that property by the person entrusted.
application: The Supreme Court examined the chargesheet and other materials on record to determine if a prima facie case was made out for the alleged offenses.

Regarding the offense under Section 323 IPC, the Court found only a "bald statement" by the complainant about being beaten, with no supporting evidence like an injury report or proof of medical treatment. It concluded the basic ingredients of the offense were not met.
For the offense under Section 384 IPC, the Court found that the essential ingredients of putting someone in fear of injury and dishonestly inducing them to deliver property were not satisfied.
Similarly, for the offense under Section 406 IPC, the Court determined that the necessary elements of entrustment of property and its subsequent dishonest misappropriation were also not satisfied.
The Court reasoned that since the ingredients for all the alleged offenses were wanting, allowing the prosecution to continue would serve no useful purpose.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had clearly fallen in error by not invoking its powers under Section 482, Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings. Because the chargesheet failed to establish a prima facie case for any of the alleged offenses, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed the FIR, chargesheet, and summoning order against the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the chargesheet submitted showed prima facie case u/ss. 323, 384 and 406, IPC for voluntarily causing hurt, for extortion and for criminal breach of trust;
appellant_arguments: The chargesheet and other materials on record do not contain the necessary ingredients to make out the offenses under Sections 323, 384, and 406 of the IPC.
The allegation for the offense under Section 323 IPC is merely a bald statement without sufficient material.

The FIR was filed on 04.09.2016, only after the appellant had already filed for dissolution of marriage and guardianship of the minor daughter on 16.05.2016, suggesting the complaint was a counter-blast.
respondent_arguments: The State of Uttar Pradesh filed a counter-affidavit, implicitly arguing that the chargesheet did disclose a prima facie case for the alleged offenses. (The second respondent-complainant did not appear to contest the matter).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court has fallen in error in not invoking the powers u/s. 482, Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings qua the appellant.
appellant_arguments: As the chargesheet fails to establish a prima facie case for the alleged offenses, the High Court should have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482, Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings to prevent an abuse of the process of law.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was correct in not quashing the proceedings as there was sufficient material to proceed with the trial.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Criminal proceedings are liable to be quashed under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code when the essential ingredients required to constitute the charged offenses are not satisfied by the accusations or materials on record. A prima facie case is not established if the allegations fail to demonstrate: (i) for an offense under Section 323 of the IPC, any material supporting the voluntary causation of hurt; (ii) for an offense under Section 384 of the IPC, the intentional putting of a person in fear of injury to dishonestly induce the delivery of property; and (iii) for an offense under Section 406 of the IPC, the entrustment of property and its subsequent dishonest misappropriation or conversion.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: After a careful review of the chargesheet and other materials on record, the court found that the necessary legal ingredients to attract the offenses under Sections 323, 384, and 406 of the I.P.C. were wanting. Consequently, the court concluded that no useful purpose would be served by allowing the criminal prosecution against the appellant to continue, and held that the High Court had erred in not exercising its power under Section 482, Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings.
legal_tests_applied: For an offense under Section 323, IPC (voluntarily causing hurt), the court required more than a 'bald statement,' looking for supporting material such as evidence of seeing a doctor, undergoing treatment, or an injury report.

For an offense under Section 384, IPC (extortion), the court applied a two-part test for the presence of the following ingredients: (i) Intentionally putting a person in fear of injury to himself or another; and (ii) Dishonestly inducing the person so put to deliver to any person any property or valuable security.

For an offense under Section 406, IPC (criminal breach of trust), the court looked for the essential ingredients of: (i) Entrusting any person with property or with any dominion over property; and (ii) The person entrusted dishonestly misappropriating, converting, using, or disposing of that property in violation of a direction of law or legal contract.

For invoking powers under Section 482, Cr.P.C., the court assessed whether the continuation of proceedings would constitute an abuse of the process of law, particularly when the ingredients of the alleged offenses are not made out from the chargesheet.
policy_considerations: It serves no useful purpose to allow a criminal prosecution to continue when the chargesheet itself demonstrates that the essential ingredients of the alleged offenses are wanting.
The High Court has a duty to invoke its powers under Section 482, Cr.P.C. to quash proceedings in order to prevent an abuse of the process of law where a prima facie case is not established.
